bib.title: SentencePiece: A simple and language independent subword tokenizer and detokenizer for Neural Text Processing

question: Can a subword tokenizer and detokenizer be built that trains directly from raw sentences, is lossless and language independent, and still matches pre-tokenized subword quality in NMT?
hypothesis: Pre-tokenization is not always necessary for subword NMT, and training on raw text is fast enough to be practical.
contributions: Open-source C++/Python/TensorFlow library implementing BPE and unigram LM subword segmentation trained directly from raw sentences
Lossless tokenization with whitespace escaped as a meta symbol
Customizable Unicode normalization (default NFKC) compiled into the model
Self-contained model file; on-the-fly API enabling subword regularization

method.summary: A tokenizer library with Normalizer, Trainer, Encoder and Decoder components. Validated by training GNMT models on KFTT English-Japanese with word, SentencePiece and SentencePiece with pre-tokenization, and by timing training and segmentation against subword-nmt.
method.task: subword tokenization for neural machine translation (English-Japanese)

datasets.name: KFTT (Kyoto Free Translation Task), Wikipedia en-ja
datasets.preprocessing: Moses tokenizer (English) and KyTea (Japanese) for pre-tokenization arms and the word model; Japanese output segmented with KyTea before BLEU

models.name: GNMT with SentencePiece (unigram LM)
models.tokenizer: SentencePiece unigram LM, with and without pre-tokenization

other.settings: generally followed Wu et al. 2016 (GNMT) settings and training procedure; only node size 512 and 6 layers changed

metrics.name: case-sensitive BLEU
metrics.definition: Papineni et al. 2002; Japanese output segmented with KyTea first

metrics.name: training and segmentation time
metrics.definition: wall time on KFTT 440k sentences, vocabulary 16k, Xeon 3.5GHz Linux

eval.protocol: single reported run per cell; no seeds or significance test reported (text says ja to en improvement from pre-tokenization 'has no significant difference' without naming a test)

evidence.quote: we changed the node and layer size of LSTM to be 512 and 6 respectively

results.claim: SentencePiece without pre-tokenization beats the word model on ja to en.
results.setup: KFTT ja to en, GNMT 6x512 LSTM, SentencePiece unigram 8k shared vocab vs word model 80k/80k, Moses/KyTea tokenizers for word model
results.table: Table 1, ja to en, rows SentencePiece 8k (shared) and Word model (baseline) 80k/80k, column BLEU

results.claim: SentencePiece beats the word model on en to ja.
results.setup: KFTT en to ja, same models as above
results.table: Table 1, en to ja, rows SentencePiece 8k (shared) and Word model (baseline) 80k/80k, column BLEU

results.claim: Pre-tokenization gives a marginal, non-significant gain on ja to en and hurts on en to ja.
results.setup: SentencePiece w/ pre-tok. vs without, 8k shared vocab
results.quote: In Japanese to English, the improvement is marginal and has no signiﬁcant difference. In English to Japanese, the BLEU score is degraded with pre-tokenization.

results.claim: On raw Japanese, SentencePiece segmentation is about 380 times faster than subword-nmt.
results.setup: KFTT 440k sentences, vocab 16k, no pre-tokenization, BPE model in SentencePiece; 5.9 s vs 216.2 s
results.quote: The segmentation speed of SentencePiece is about 380 times faster than that of subword-nmt in this setting.
results.note: 216.2/5.9 is about 37, not 380; the 380 figure does not follow from Table 2 as printed

results.claim: Segmentation speed is fast enough for on-the-fly use.
results.quote: The segmentation speed of SentencePiece is around 21k and 74k sentences/sec. in English and Japanese respectively

results.claim: Training on raw Japanese takes 217.3 s with SentencePiece vs 528.0 s with subword-nmt.
results.table: Table 2, Train, Pre-tok no, Japanese, SentencePiece 217.3 vs subword-nmt 528.0

results.claim: BPE and unigram LM show almost comparable speed performance.
results.quote: We found that BPE and unigram language models show almost comparable performance.

results.claim: Naive BPE segmentation is O(N^2); SentencePiece uses a binary-heap O(N log N) algorithm.
results.quote: SentencePiece adopts an O(N log(N)) algorithm in which the merged symbols are managed by a binary heap (priority queue).

limits: One language pair (en-ja) and one small corpus (440k sentences); no seeds or variance reported.
Training hyperparameters other than layers and nodes are not given; deferred to GNMT.
Word model uses 80k vocab vs 8k for SentencePiece, so vocab size is confounded with segmentation method.
SentencePiece implements only a subset of NFKC (no full CCC reordering).
Speed numbers are for 2018 Xeon hardware.

terms.definition: Decode(Encode(Normalize(text))) = Normalize(text); all information to reproduce the normalized text is preserved in the encoder's output

lineage.work: Neural machine translation of rare words with subword units (Sennrich et al.)
A call for clarity in reporting BLEU scores (Post)

problems: Text uses ASCII underscore where the paper's meta symbol is U+2581.
Sec 4.2 claims 380x segmentation speedup but Table 2 gives 216.2/5.9 which is about 37x.
